question: What four access or information-exchange levels are in the assigned paper’s taxonomy, and what benefits does it associate with collaboration?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (PDF p. 2, introduction)
reference_answer: The paper lists API-level, text-level, logit-level, and weight-level collaboration. It associates multi-LLM protocols with benefits including pluralism, democratization, efficiency, and adaptability.
required_answer_points: Four levels exactly; hierarchy is based on access/information exchange; at least two benefits from p. 2.
reviewer_notes: Synthesis item intentionally spans the abstract and introduction. Attribute benefits as the paper’s argument.

question: What limitations of relying on one general-purpose LLM motivate the assigned paper’s collaboration proposal, and why does it say simply scaling one model is insufficient?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P3 (PDF p. 3, section 2)
reference_answer: The authors argue that one model may underrepresent real-world data distributions, heterogeneous skills, and pluralistic populations. The paper further argues that representation of populations requires solutions beyond simply scaling data for one general-purpose model and notes that single-model reliance also concentrates development in a homogeneous team.
required_answer_points: Underrepresented distributions/skills/populations; scaling data alone is insufficient; single-team development creates a further representation concern.
reviewer_notes: Paraphrase a position paper’s argument; do not present it as a causal experimental finding.

question: How does Du et al.’s debate procedure work, and what evidence in the paper’s opening pages illustrates the tasks and comparison used?
passage_ids: P1 (Du et al. PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (PDF p. 2, figure/caption and introduction)
reference_answer: Multiple model instances propose answers and reasoning and debate over rounds toward a common answer. The paper’s opening results discuss six benchmarks spanning factuality, reasoning, and QA, and compare a single-model baseline with multi-model debate; it says multiple agents and multiple rounds matter for best performance.
required_answer_points: Multi-instance proposals/reasoning; repeated debate; common answer; six benchmarks/tasks; single-model comparison; role of both multiple agents and rounds.
reviewer_notes: Use the source’s own description. Do not say our prototype reproduced these results.

question: How does the assigned paper’s taxonomy differ from Du et al.’s concrete debate approach, and what shared idea connects them?
passage_ids: P1 (assigned paper PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (Du et al. PDF p. 2, introduction)
reference_answer: The assigned paper organizes collaboration broadly by access and information exchange (API, text, logits, weights). Du et al. describe one concrete approach: multiple instances exchange proposed answers/reasoning over rounds and converge. Both treat interaction among model instances as a way to combine diverse answers or reasoning rather than relying only on one isolated response.
required_answer_points: Taxonomy versus concrete procedure; four categories; multi-round debate; common answer; shared multi-model collaboration idea.
reviewer_notes: Clearly distinguish a conceptual taxonomy from the empirical method; keep “diverse” grounded in the Du paper’s opening discussion.

question: In Debate or Vote, which component explains most gains attributed to multi-agent debate, and what theoretical explanation do the authors provide?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (PDF p. 2, introduction)
reference_answer: The authors report that majority voting alone accounts for most gains typically attributed to MAD across their seven NLP benchmarks. Their framework treats debate as a stochastic process that induces a martingale over belief trajectories, so debate alone does not improve expected correctness. Page 2 explains that majority voting aggregates agent outputs before debate rounds.
required_answer_points: Majority voting; seven benchmarks; pre-debate aggregation; martingale over belief trajectories; qualified implication about expected correctness.
reviewer_notes: Keep conclusion limited to the paper’s theoretical framework and experimental setup.

question: What problem do targeted interventions address in Debate or Vote, and why might majority voting be a practical alternative?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (PDF p. 2, introduction)
reference_answer: The paper proposes interventions that bias belief updates toward correction to make debate more effective. It notes that if gains primarily come from aggregating diverse independent outputs, majority voting may achieve much of the benefit with less computational and architectural overhead.
required_answer_points: Correction-biased belief updates; diversity/independent aggregation rationale; lower overhead as motivation; majority voting can be strong.
reviewer_notes: Preserve the paper’s conditional framing (“if most gain stems from ensembling”).

question: What decision protocols and task categories does Voting or Consensus study, and what task-specific advantages does its abstract report?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (PDF p. 2, methods overview)
reference_answer: The study compares seven decision protocols, including voting and unanimity consensus, across knowledge and reasoning tasks; page 2 specifies three consensus and four voting methods. It reports voting protocols perform 13.2% better on reasoning tasks and consensus protocols 2.8% better on knowledge tasks than other decision protocols.
required_answer_points: Seven protocols; three consensus/four voting variants; knowledge and reasoning task categories; 13.2% reasoning voting result; 2.8% knowledge consensus result.
reviewer_notes: Include the comparator and task category; these are paper-reported figures, not our findings.

question: What design choices affect outcomes in Voting or Consensus, and what are AAD and CI intended to add?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (PDF p. 2, methods overview)
reference_answer: The paper reports that adding agents improves performance while adding more rounds before voting reduces it. AAD has agents independently draft initial solutions before interaction; CI uses iterative refinement while limiting excessive communication. The methods aim to improve answer diversity; the abstract reports gains up to 3.3% for AAD and 7.4% for CI.
required_answer_points: Agent count and discussion-round trends; AAD full name and independent drafts; CI full name and iterative refinement; diversity motivation; qualified maxima.
reviewer_notes: Do not turn “up to” results into average gains.

question: How does the scalable-oversight study distinguish debate, consultancy, and direct QA, and what task types does it evaluate?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P2 (PDF p. 2, Figure 1 caption)
reference_answer: Debate uses two AIs competing to convince a judge; consultancy uses one AI to convince a judge who asks questions; direct QA has the judge answer without AI assistance. The study includes extractive QA, closed QA, and multimodal reasoning tasks, with the figure describing their input distinctions.
required_answer_points: Correct definitions for all three protocols; all three task types; accurate summary of source/article availability distinction from the figure.
reviewer_notes: Definitions based on the study’s own protocol descriptions.

question: What does the scalable-oversight study report about debate versus consultancy and debate versus direct QA, and how do the findings vary with information asymmetry?
passage_ids: P1 (PDF p. 1, abstract); P3 (PDF p. 3, main findings)
reference_answer: Debate outperforms consultancy across tasks in the assigned-role setup. Against direct QA, debate outperforms on extractive QA with information asymmetry, while results are mixed for other tasks without that asymmetry.
required_answer_points: Consultancy comparison and setup; direct QA comparison; extractive QA with information asymmetry; mixed results on other tasks.
reviewer_notes: Retain all task and protocol qualifications; report as published findings.
